result.summary: Iris is sent to fetch Eilithyia so that Leto can give birth on Delos. Apollo is born, fed by Themis, and declares his gifts, and Delos rejoices. The hymn then praises the Ionian festival on Delos and the Delian girls, and the poet asks them to remember him as the blind singer of Chios.

scenes.title: Iris fetches Eilithyia
scenes.summary: The goddesses send Iris to bring Eilithyia with the promise of a great necklace, and Iris persuades her away from Hera.
scenes.stakes: Leto's labour is stalled unless Eilithyia comes; Hera might turn her aside.

scenes.title: Birth of Apollo
scenes.summary: Leto bears Apollo on Delos, Themis feeds him divine food, and he bursts his bands and announces his gifts. Delos is filled with gold in joy.
scenes.stakes: Leto's painful labour and the newborn god's establishment.

scenes.title: Ionian festival at Delos
scenes.summary: Apollo's delight in Delos is described, with the Ionians' gathering and the Delian girls' marvellous singing.

scenes.title: Poet's farewell to the maidens
scenes.summary: The poet bids the girls farewell and asks them to name him the blind man of Chios, promising to spread their fame.

alias_notes.explanation: Phoebus is a common epithet of Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Apollo's first words declare his domains: music, archery and prophecy.
The poet's famous self-description as the blind man of Chios, traditionally Homer.

analysis.text: The birth shows Apollo's divine power at once: he shakes off swaddling and claims his roles, making Delos honoured among islands.
The passage reflects the Ionian festival on Delos with athletics, dance and song, and the closing lines are the source of the tradition that Homer was a blind Chian.

legacy.text: The reference to a blind singer from Chios, quoted by Thucydides as Homer's, fed the ancient tradition of Homer's blindness and Chian origin.

fun_facts.text: Thucydides quoted this hymn as evidence of the ancient Delian festival and attributed it to Homer.

language_notes.text: A cubit is an ancient measure of length, roughly the distance from elbow to fingertip, about half a metre; the necklace is enormous.
"Sore travail" means painful labour; Eilithyia is the goddess of childbirth, so her arrival is what allows the birth to begin.
Nectar and ambrosia are the food and drink of the gods, conferring immortality and strength.
"Golden cords" and "bands" are the swaddling bands put on the newborn; Apollo bursts free of them at once.
"Long robed Ionians" refers to the Greek people of the central Aegean coast and islands, who gathered at Delos for festivals.
The final clause appears corrupt or garbled in this text; the poet's sense is that he will spread the maidens' fame in his travels.

context_notes.text: Leto's labour was prolonged because jealous Hera kept Eilithyia away; the goddesses use a bribe to get around her.
Themis is the goddess of divine law and order, here acting as nurse to the newborn god.
Cynthus is the hill on Delos, which gave Apollo and Artemis the title Cynthian.
The "blind man of Chios" is the poet's self-description, later taken as a claim that Homer composed this hymn.

literary_notes.text: Comparing the two goddesses to shy wild-doves conveys their quick, timid, fluttering haste on their journey.
The earth laughing for joy beneath Leto makes nature share in the happiness of the birth.
The narrator turns suddenly to address Phoebus directly, giving the hymn an intimate tone of worship.
Delos blossoming like a mountain-top with woodland flowers presents the island as flourishing with joy at being chosen.
Saying the gathered Ionians seem deathless and unageing exaggerates to show the splendour of the festival.
The poet has the girls describe him in their words, making his self-portrait seem modest while praising his songs as supreme.
